lessonTitle: Peripheral Nerve Injuries of the Lower Limb

blocks.text: After a night in a plaster cast that ended just below the knee, a man finds that his foot slaps the ground when he walks and his toes catch on the carpet. He cannot lift the front of the foot, and the skin over the top of the foot is numb. A nerve that runs right against the bone just below the knee explains it.

blocks.markdown: In the lower limb three nerves are injured especially often: the **common fibular nerve** (exposed at the neck of the fibula), the **superior gluteal nerve** (which stabilises the pelvis in walking) and the **femoral and sciatic nerves** (which supply the large muscle groups of the thigh). As in the upper limb, the pattern of weakness and numbness points to the nerve and the level of the lesion, and the effect on walking, the gait, is often the first clue.

blocks.title: Common fibular nerve
blocks.text: One of the two terminal branches of the sciatic nerve (the other is the tibial nerve). It leaves the popliteal fossa along the medial border of biceps femoris, winds around the neck of the fibula, where it lies subcutaneously, and divides into the superficial and deep fibular nerves. The superficial fibular nerve supplies the fibular (peroneal) muscles, which evert the foot; the deep fibular nerve supplies the extensors of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus), which dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes.

blocks.markdown: **Injury at the fibular neck.** The nerve is vulnerable here because it is superficial and lies directly on bone. It is damaged by fractures of the fibular neck, direct blows (for example a car bumper), tight plaster casts or bandages, and prolonged leg crossing. The result is **foot drop**: weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion. The foot hangs plantarflexed and inverted, because the unopposed posterior and medial muscles, supplied by the tibial nerve, dominate. The patient compensates by lifting the knee higher than normal during the swing phase to clear the toes: a **high-stepping (steppage) gait**. There is sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot, and over the first web space if the deep fibular nerve is involved.

blocks.title: From foot drop to nerve
blocks.prompt: A patient cannot dorsiflex or evert the foot, has numbness over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, but can plantarflex and invert the foot. Name the nerve and the likely level of the lesion.

steps.text: Dorsiflexion is by the anterior compartment (deep fibular nerve) and eversion by the lateral compartment (superficial fibular nerve), so both fibular branches are involved.
Plantarflexion and inversion are by the tibial nerve, which is intact.
Both branches arise from the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula, so the lesion lies at or above this point but distal to the sciatic division.

blocks.answer: The common fibular nerve, at the neck of the fibula.

blocks.markdown: **Superior gluteal nerve and the Trendelenburg sign.** The superior gluteal nerve (L4 to S1) supplies **gluteus medius**, **gluteus minimus** and tensor fasciae latae. In normal walking, when one leg is lifted, the gluteus medius and minimus of the **standing** leg contract to hold the pelvis level, preventing it from tilting towards the lifted side. If the nerve is injured (for example by a misplaced injection or in hip surgery) these muscles are weak. When the patient stands on the affected leg, the **pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side**: this is a positive **Trendelenburg sign**. In walking the patient tilts the trunk towards the weak side to keep the centre of gravity over the stance leg, giving a waddling or Trendelenburg gait.

rows: Pelvis drops on the side opposite the lesion in stance on the affected leg (positive Trendelenburg sign)
Quadriceps (knee extension), sartorius, weak hip flexion
Anterior thigh and medial leg (saphenous nerve)
Knee gives way, difficulty climbing stairs; knee jerk lost
Hamstrings and all muscles below the knee
All skin below the knee except the medial leg (saphenous nerve)
Foot drop with weak knee flexion; knee extension preserved
blocks.caption: Comparing common lower limb nerve lesions.

blocks.title: Positive Trendelenburg test
blocks.prompt: When a patient stands on the right leg, the left side of the pelvis drops. Which side is the lesion, which nerve, and which muscles are weak?

steps.text: The pelvis drops on the side of the lifted (unsupported) leg, which is the left.
The muscles that fail to hold the pelvis level are those of the standing leg, the right.
The gluteus medius and minimus of the right side are therefore weak, and they are supplied by the right superior gluteal nerve.

blocks.answer: A right superior gluteal nerve lesion, with weak right gluteus medius and minimus.

blocks.title: Distinguishing sciatic from femoral lesions
blocks.text: A femoral nerve lesion paralyses knee extension (quadriceps) and weakens hip flexion, and loses sensation over the anterior thigh and the medial leg (saphenous nerve). A sciatic lesion spares knee extension and the medial leg skin but paralyses the hamstrings and all muscles below the knee, and causes sensory loss over the rest of the leg and foot. Test knee extension, knee flexion, ankle movements and the skin of the medial and lateral leg.

items: Common fibular nerve at the fibular neck: foot drop, high-stepping gait, loss of eversion and dorsiflexion.
Superior gluteal nerve: weak abduction at the hip and a positive Trendelenburg sign.
Femoral nerve: weak knee extension, numb anterior thigh and medial leg.
Sciatic nerve: hamstrings and all muscles below the knee paralysed; knee extension preserved.

blocks.title: Which side drops?
blocks.text: In Trendelenburg testing the pelvis drops on the side that is lifted, not on the side that is weak. The weak muscles are on the standing leg. Remember that the muscles of the standing leg are the ones doing the work.

points: The common fibular nerve is injured at the neck of the fibula, causing foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion) and a high-stepping gait.
Superior gluteal nerve injury weakens gluteus medius and minimus, causing the pelvis to drop on the side opposite the lesion when standing on the affected leg (Trendelenburg sign).
Femoral lesions affect knee extension and the anterior thigh and medial leg; sciatic lesions spare knee extension but affect the hamstrings and all muscles below the knee.

questions.stem: A man develops foot drop after wearing a tight cast below the knee. Which nerve is most likely injured?

distractorRationale.b: Tibial nerve injury would weaken plantarflexion, not dorsiflexion.
distractorRationale.c: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps.
distractorRationale.d: The superior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteal muscles.

questions.explanation: The common fibular nerve is superficial at the neck of the fibula and is easily compressed. Its injury paralyses the dorsiflexors and evertors, causing foot drop.

questions.stem: Which movements are lost after injury of the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula?

distractorRationale.b: Plantarflexion and inversion are by the tibial nerve and are preserved.
distractorRationale.c: Knee extension and hip flexion depend on the femoral nerve.
distractorRationale.d: Hip abduction depends on the superior gluteal nerve.

questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve supplies the dorsiflexors and the superficial fibular nerve supplies the evertors, both from the common fibular nerve. The foot therefore hangs plantarflexed and inverted.

questions.stem: Which gait abnormality would you expect in a patient with a common fibular nerve injury?

options.text: Dragging the whole leg without hip movement

distractorRationale.b: A waddling or Trendelenburg gait results from superior gluteal nerve injury.
distractorRationale.c: Loss of knee extension suggests a femoral nerve lesion.
distractorRationale.d: This does not follow from isolated fibular nerve injury.

questions.explanation: The patient cannot dorsiflex the foot, so the toes would drag during swing. To clear the ground they lift the knee higher than normal, a high-stepping gait.

questions.stem: A patient stands on the right leg and the left side of the pelvis drops. Which lesion is most likely?

distractorRationale.b: The left muscles are not working during right-leg stance, so the left nerve is not the cause.
distractorRationale.c: A femoral nerve lesion would not cause pelvic drop.
distractorRationale.d: A fibular nerve lesion causes foot drop.

questions.explanation: During right-leg stance the right gluteus medius and minimus hold the pelvis level. If they are weak, the left side of the pelvis drops, so the lesion is on the right.

questions.stem: Which muscles are weakened in a superior gluteal nerve lesion?

distractorRationale.b: Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve.
distractorRationale.c: The hamstrings are supplied by the sciatic nerve.
distractorRationale.d: The quadriceps is supplied by the femoral nerve.

questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae. These muscles abduct the thigh and stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance.

questions.stem: A patient cannot extend the knee and has numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg. Which nerve is damaged?

distractorRationale.b: A sciatic lesion spares knee extension.
distractorRationale.d: A fibular lesion causes foot drop.

questions.explanation: Knee extension depends on quadriceps (femoral nerve), and the anterior thigh and medial leg are supplied by the femoral nerve and its saphenous branch. A sciatic lesion would spare these.

questions.stem: True or false: a complete sciatic nerve lesion in the gluteal region leaves knee extension intact.

distractorRationale.b: Knee extension is by the quadriceps, supplied by the femoral nerve, which is not affected.

questions.explanation: Knee extension is produced by quadriceps, supplied by the femoral nerve. A sciatic lesion paralyses the hamstrings and all muscles below the knee but spares the quadriceps.

questions.stem: After a posterior dislocation of the hip, a man has weak knee flexion, foot drop, no plantarflexion and loss of sensation over the leg except the medial side. Which statement best explains the findings?

options.text: Sciatic nerve injury, with the medial leg spared because the saphenous nerve is from the femoral nerve
Femoral nerve injury, with the medial leg spared because of the obturator nerve

questions.correctOptionText: Sciatic nerve injury, with the medial leg spared because the saphenous nerve is from the femoral nerve

distractorRationale.b: A femoral lesion would affect knee extension and the medial leg.
distractorRationale.c: A common fibular lesion would not cause loss of plantarflexion and knee flexion.
distractorRationale.d: This nerve causes pelvic tilt, not these deficits.

questions.explanation: Loss of hamstrings and all muscles below the knee means the sciatic nerve is damaged proximally. The medial leg is supplied by the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, so it is spared.

questions.stem: Explain how damage to the superior gluteal nerve produces a positive Trendelenburg sign.
markingGuide: Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae.
In single-leg stance these muscles on the standing side hold the pelvis level.
With the nerve damaged these muscles are weak, so the pelvis drops on the opposite (lifted) side.
The patient may tilt the trunk towards the weak side to compensate, giving a waddling gait.
The lesion is on the same side as the standing leg being tested.
questions.explanation: The stance-side abductors prevent the pelvis from tilting during single-leg support. Weakness makes the unsupported side sag, which is the sign.

questions.stem: Distinguish a sciatic nerve lesion from a femoral nerve lesion in terms of the motor and sensory loss produced.
markingGuide: Femoral: weak knee extension (quadriceps) and hip flexion; sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg (saphenous nerve); knee jerk lost.
Sciatic: weak knee flexion (hamstrings) and paralysis of all muscles below the knee; foot drop.
Sciatic: sensory loss below the knee except the medial leg.
Knee extension is preserved in a sciatic lesion.
The medial leg is spared in a sciatic lesion because the saphenous nerve is a branch of the femoral nerve.
questions.explanation: Each nerve supplies a distinct set of muscles and skin. Comparing knee extension with knee flexion and ankle movement quickly separates the two lesions.
